kp.k: AI supports self-representation, with mixed reported outcomes
kp.d: NBC News reports that litigants increasingly use generative AI to navigate procedure, interpret legal language and prepare cases, sometimes foregoing lawyers. Its reporting draws on interviews with over 15 pro se litigants, legal professionals, nonprofit leaders, AI startups and legal research companies, rather than a systematic measurement of adoption or success rates. Interviewees describe both successful assistance and penalties for inaccurate filings.
qs: To understand the role of AI in self-represented, or pro se, litigation, NBC News spoke with over 15 pro se litigants, legal professionals, nonprofit leaders, AI startups and legal research companies.
In interviews, lawyers and litigants described AI as producing mixed results in court.
Many are eschewing lawyers altogether, representing themselves in court with AI as their primary guide.

kp.k: Tenant attributes successful eviction appeal to inexpensive AI assistance
kp.d: After losing a jury trial with legal assistance, Lynn White used ChatGPT and Perplexity to identify possible procedural errors, research laws, plan actions and draft court responses. The article reports that she overturned her eviction notice after several months and avoided roughly $55,000 in penalties and more than $18,000 in overdue rent. White attributes her success to AI; the account does not establish AI's independent causal effect. She initially used free ChatGPT before paying $20 a month, alongside Perplexity Pro at $20 a month.
qs: The chatbot helped White identify potential errors in a judge’s procedural decisions, chart out possible courses of action, research applicable laws and draft responses to the court.
Several months of litigation later, White managed to overturn her eviction notice and avoid roughly $55,000 in penalties and more than $18,000 in overdue rent.
I never, ever, ever, ever could have won this appeal without AI.

kp.k: Debt litigant uses AI for drafting and adversarial critique
kp.d: Staci Dennett describes using ChatGPT to respond to an unpaid-debt summons through templates, drafted arguments and repeated requests to identify flaws in her reasoning. The passage reports settlement savings exceeding $2,000, but switches the subject's name to White, making attribution of that outcome internally inconsistent.
qs: The bot provided templates and drafted arguments for her responses, with Dennett regularly asking it to find potential errors in her logic.
I would tell ChatGPT to pretend it was a Harvard Law professor and to rip my arguments apart
White ultimately negotiated a settlement and saved over $2,000 compared to her original debt, which she said was a partial victory she attributes largely to AI.

kp.k: Provider restrictions coexist with readily available chatbot legal advice
kp.d: The article contrasts company policies discouraging professional reliance or requiring regulatory compliance with chatbots' willingness to answer legal questions. It reports that most provide advice without warnings beyond general accuracy disclaimers. Perplexity's spokesperson acknowledges imperfect accuracy while asserting a commitment to improving it; OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and xAI did not respond to requests for comment.
qs: Don’t rely on the Services for medical, legal, financial, or other professional advice. Any content regarding those topics is provided for informational purposes only and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified professional.

Yet when asked legal questions, most chatbots will respond and provide legal advice without any warnings beyond ever-present, fine-print disclaimers noting that generative AI answers may not be accurate.
We don’t claim to be 100% accurate, but we do claim to be the only company who works on it relentlessly.

kp.k: Faulty AI filings expose litigants to dismissal and sanctions
kp.d: Paralegal Meagan Holmes reports encountering nonexistent authorities and arguments insufficient to state claims. The article describes Jack Owoc's sanction for a motion containing 11 fabricated case citations: 10 hours of community service and mandatory disclosure of AI use in future filings in the case. Owoc says limited finances prompted his AI use and emphasizes checking its work.
qs: Most of the time, we get them dismissed for failure to state an actual claim, because a lot of times it’s just kind of, not to be rude, but nonsense.

kp.k: Court incident database records accelerating, incompletely observed AI problems
kp.d: Damien Charlotin's database contains 282 U.S. cases and more than 130 from other countries dating back to 2023; he says incidents accelerated around spring 2025. These are court-addressed instances of established or alleged AI use, not measured model error rates or a comprehensive census. Most entries arrive through lawyers or researchers, and the article says the majority of recorded hallucinations involve pro se litigants, though lawyers also contribute.
qs: He’s documented 282 such cases in the U.S. and more than 130 from other countries dating back to 2023.
It really started to accelerate around the spring of 2025
It only tracks cases where the established or alleged use of AI was directly addressed by the court, and Charlotin said most of its entries are referred to him by lawyers or other researchers.
So far, the majority of AI hallucinations in Charlotin’s database come from pro se litigants, but many have also come from lawyers themselves.

kp.k: Existing authorities can still carry fabricated quotations or misrepresentations
kp.d: Charlotin distinguishes nonexistent cases, false quotations from real cases and misrepresentation of existing authorities, describing the last as harder to detect. Earl Takefman recounts discovering that asking ChatGPT for actual quotations did not prevent fabrication. After a late-August demand to explain why sanctions should not issue, the court accepted his apology without sanctions. He reports subsequently comparing outputs across chatbots and checking case existence through Google.
qs: You got the fabricated case law, and that’s quite easy to spot, because the case does not exist.
And then there is misrepresented case law. That’s much harder, because you’re citing something that exists but you’re totally misrepresenting it.
Surely they would never make up an actual quotation.’ And it turns out they were making that up too!
The court accepted Takefman’s apology and did not apply sanctions.
Then, I put all of the cases into Google to do one last check to make sure that the cases are real.

kp.k: Lawyers retain verification duties despite AI assistance
kp.d: The article reports a California attorney's $10,000 fine earlier that month for an appeal containing 21 hallucinated quotations out of 23 quotations from cited cases. CalMatters is credited with describing it as apparently the largest-ever fine over AI fabrications. Attorney Robert Freund treats reliance on fabricated arguments as a breach of fundamental professional responsibilities, distinguishing lawyers' obligations from the financial pressures facing unrepresented litigants.
qs: Earlier this month, a California court ordered an attorney to pay a $10,000 fine for filing a state court appeal in which 21 of the 23 quotes from cited cases were hallucinated by ChatGPT.
It appears to be the largest-ever fine issued over AI fabrications, according to CalMatters.
What I can’t understand is an attorney betraying the most fundamental parts of our responsibilities to our clients … and making these arguments that are based on total fabrication.

kp.k: AI-enabled filing volume creates access and court-burden tensions
kp.d: Freund says inaccurate AI filings consume courts' and opponents' resources and sometimes continue after judicial warnings. Matthew Garces credits AI with enabling him to manage 28 federal civil suits, including 10 active appeals and several Supreme Court petitions. Following filings citing nonexistent cases, a Fifth Circuit panel warned him a second time against abusive filings; another magistrate recommended filing restrictions and vexatious-litigant classification. Garces nevertheless frames AI as overcoming financial barriers to court access.
qs: Freund, who runs a law firm in Los Angeles, said the influx of AI hallucinations wastes both the court’s and the opposing party’s time by forcing them to use up resources identifying factual inaccuracies.
is currently involved in 28 federal civil suits, including 10 active appeals and several petitions to the Supreme Court.

A magistrate judge in another of Garces’ cases also recommended that he be banned from filing any lawsuits without the express authorization of a more senior judge, and that Garces be classified as “a vexatious litigant.”

AI provides access to the courthouse doors that money often keeps closed. Managing nearly 30 federal suits on my own would be nearly impossible without AI tools to organize, research and prepare filings.

kp.k: Legal clinics teach AI use and output checking
kp.d: Some pro bono clinics are teaching self-represented clients to use AI without providing direct legal advice. Public Counsel supervising attorney Zoe Dolan helped create a Los Angeles County class the previous year covering document-generation prompts, fact-checking and chatbot cross-checking. The article reports that several participants, including White, subsequently won cases while using AI; Dolan expresses optimism about expanding advocates' impact.
qs: some pro bono legal clinics are now trying to teach their self-representing clients to use AI in ways that help rather than harm them — without offering direct legal advice.
The class taught participants how to use various prompts to create documents, how to fact-check the AI systems’ outputs and how to use chatbots to verify other chatbots’ work.
Several of the litigants who took the class, including White, have gone on to win their cases while using AI.
The amount of impact that any one advocate can now have is only sort of limited by our imagination and organizational structures.

kp.k: Professional augmentation depends on expertise, confidentiality and manual checking
kp.d: Attorney Andrew Montez reports using AI as a research and brainstorming starting point, excluding real client names and confidential information and manually checking every citation. He says AI enables faster, better-researched briefs but cannot replace his own research and analysis. His claim that all attorneys will need AI to remain competitive is a prediction. He considers most pro se cases too complex for AI alone, while envisioning greater future success particularly in small claims courts.
qs: He said he never inputs real client names or confidential information, and he checks every citation manually.
While AI cannot substitute for his own legal research and analysis, Montez said, these systems enable lawyers to write better-researched briefs more quickly.
Going forward in the legal profession, all attorneys will have to use AI in some way or another. Otherwise they will be outgunned

As for pro se litigants without legal expertise, Montez said he believes most cases are too complex for AI alone to understand sufficient context and provide good enough analysis to help someone succeed in court.
But he noted that he could envision a future in which more people will use AI to successfully represent themselves, especially in small claims courts.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article describes growing AI-assisted self-representation with mixed outcomes: affordable research and drafting support can help litigants succeed, but inaccurate filings can cause dismissals, sanctions and additional court workload. Interviewees also predict competitive advantages for lawyers using verified AI output.
pts.d: Perlo and Yang report that increasing numbers of litigants use AI as their primary legal guide, sometimes instead of a lawyer. Lynn White attributes her successful eviction appeal to ChatGPT and Perplexity, which helped identify possible procedural errors, research laws, plan litigation and draft responses. The article also presents Staci Dennett's use of ChatGPT to respond to a debt claim and negotiate a settlement as a partial success. Matthew Garces argues that AI expands courthouse access and enables him to manage nearly 30 federal suits. Conversely, paralegal Meagan Holmes says AI-assisted litigants submit nonexistent authorities and legally deficient claims that her side often gets dismissed. Attorney Robert Freund says identifying fabrications consumes court and opposing-party resources, sometimes without stopping repeated defective filings. The article reports that hallucinations expose both self-represented litigants and lawyers to penalties. Public Counsel supervising attorney Zoe Dolan describes AI as greatly expanding an advocate's potential impact; her clinic teaches self-represented litigants to use it more carefully. Attorney Andrew Montez says AI helps lawyers produce better-researched briefs faster when used as a starting point rather than a substitute for legal analysis. He predicts that all attorneys will eventually need some AI use to remain competitive, while treating successful AI-assisted self-representation in small claims as a future possibility rather than a general present capability.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of interviews, individual litigation outcomes, reported court decisions and a non-exhaustive database of AI-related court incidents; the broader adoption and competitive predictions rest primarily on practitioner experience.
pts.d: NBC News says it interviewed over 15 pro se litigants, legal professionals, nonprofit leaders, AI startups and legal research companies. White reportedly overturned her eviction notice and avoided roughly $55,000 in penalties and more than $18,000 in overdue rent; her claim that AI was indispensable is her own attribution. In the Dennett narrative, the article reports a settlement saving more than $2,000, but the settlement sentence unexpectedly names White, creating an internal attribution inconsistency. Several participants in Dolan's class, including White, reportedly won cases while using AI; the source supplies no class size or comparative success rate. Legal researcher Damien Charlotin's database contains 282 U.S. cases and more than 130 elsewhere dating to 2023, with a majority of its hallucination incidents involving pro se litigants. These are tracked court incidents, not measured model error rates or a representative estimate of AI use. Specific adverse examples include Jack Owoc's motion containing 11 fabricated citations, followed by 10 hours of community service and an AI-disclosure requirement; Earl Takefman's repeated citation of a nonexistent case and discovery of fabricated quotations, followed by a sanctions inquiry but no sanctions after his apology; and an attorney ordered to pay $10,000 after 21 of 23 case quotations in an appeal were hallucinated. Garces' numerous filings and appellate warnings illustrate increased filing capacity alongside concerns about abusive litigation. Holmes, Freund and Montez rely on their professional observations; Montez's claim that attorneys will need AI to remain competitive is a prediction, not a benchmark finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes developments current in 2025, with court incidents tracked since 2023 and reported acceleration in spring 2025. Its optimistic claims are qualified by human verification, legal expertise and case complexity; its future predictions have no fixed deadline.
pts.d: Holmes describes seeing more pro se litigants over the preceding year, while Montez describes frequent AI use by self-represented opponents over the preceding six months. Charlotin dates acceleration in tracked incidents to spring 2025. White's successful litigation took several months and avoided eviction in the article's publication year. Dolan helped establish the training class the previous year. The source does not specify the calendar dates corresponding to every relative reference. Montez's current positive assessment is conditional: he uses AI for initial research or brainstorming, omits real client names and confidential information, checks every citation manually, and retains responsibility for research and analysis. He believes most cases are too complex for AI alone to understand enough context to help a nonexpert succeed, but envisions more successful self-representation particularly in small claims. Owoc likewise emphasizes checking AI work. Takefman describes cross-checking different chatbots and then searching Google for case existence; the article reports this as his response to errors, not as a demonstrated guarantee of legal accuracy. Charlotin distinguishes fabricated cases and quotations from the harder-to-detect misrepresentation of genuine authorities. The authors note that company restrictions and disclaimers do not necessarily prevent chatbots from answering legal questions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are self-represented civil litigants with limited access to counsel, lawyers and nonprofit advocates, and courts and opposing parties required to scrutinize AI-generated filings.
pts.d: Individuals facing eviction, debt collection, housing disputes and other civil matters gain access to drafting, research, procedural explanations and document organization without necessarily retaining counsel. White initially used free ChatGPT and later paid $20 monthly for its premium service; she also used Perplexity Pro at $20 monthly. These examples concern individual access to legal help rather than enterprise legal cost savings. The same litigants bear the risk of dismissals, sanctions, disclosure requirements and filing restrictions when they rely on fabricated or inadequate material; Takefman says self-representation does not excuse misleading citations. Lawyers may gain speed and research support, but remain exposed to financial penalties and failures of responsibility to clients if they do not verify output. Montez predicts a competitive disadvantage for non-adopting attorneys, without claiming quantified job losses or changes to firm staffing. Nonprofit legal clinics are adding AI-literacy and fact-checking instruction for self-represented users without providing direct legal advice in those classes. Courts, opposing counsel and their clients must spend resources identifying inaccuracies, and high-volume AI-assisted filing can increase that burden. Consumer chatbot providers supply the tools, but the article does not present them as law firms or alternative legal service providers delivering the litigation work.
